@graph.name: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome Warning Signs
@graph.headline: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome Warning Signs

mainEntity.name: What are the first signs of OHSS?

acceptedAnswer.text: Early signs include bloating, mild abdominal discomfort, nausea and slight weight gain a few days after the trigger. Severe signs include rapid weight gain, severe pain, vomiting, breathlessness and reduced urination.

mainEntity.name: How long does OHSS last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mild OHSS usually settles in about a week. If pregnancy occurs, symptoms can last longer, sometimes two weeks or more. Severe cases need medical care.

mainEntity.name: Can OHSS be prevented?

acceptedAnswer.text: Risk can be reduced by individualised medicine doses, careful monitoring, special trigger options and freezing all embryos for later transfer. Your specialist selects the safest protocol for you.

mainEntity.name: Does OHSS affect the chance of pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: OHSS itself does not necessarily reduce the chance of pregnancy, but doctors may freeze embryos and delay transfer until you recover. Pregnancy can prolong OHSS symptoms.

mainEntity.name: Should I go to hospital for bloating after egg collection?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mild bloating is common. Go to the hospital or call your clinic for rapid weight gain, severe pain, vomiting, shortness of breath, very little urine or leg swelling.

@graph.name: Ovulation Tracking How to Know Your Fertile Window
@graph.headline: Ovulation Tracking How to Know Your Fertile Window

mainEntity.name: When is the best time to get pregnant in a cycle?

acceptedAnswer.text: The best chance of pregnancy is in the fertile window, the few days leading up to and including ovulation. Intercourse every one to two days in this window is recommended.

mainEntity.name: How accurate are ovulation kits?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ovulation kits detect the LH surge and are fairly reliable for most women, but results can be confusing in conditions like PCOS or when taking certain medicines. Ultrasound monitoring is more precise.

mainEntity.name: Can I get pregnant if my cycle is irregular?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but ovulation timing is less predictable, and irregular cycles may signal underlying issues. See a doctor if your cycles are very irregular or you have been trying for a year.

mainEntity.name: What is follicular monitoring?

acceptedAnswer.text: Follicular monitoring uses serial ultrasounds to watch the growth of the egg-containing follicle and check when it is ready to release the egg. It helps time intercourse or treatments like IUI.

mainEntity.name: Does basal body temperature predict ovulation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Temperature rises after ovulation, so it confirms ovulation in retrospect rather than predicting it. It is useful for seeing your pattern over several cycles.

@graph.headline: PCOS After 30: Age, Metabolic Health and Fertility Planning

mainEntity.name: Is it too late to try for a baby with PCOS at 30 or older?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Age matters, but many women over 30 with PCOS do conceive. What matters more is how far along your planning is. Early checks of ovulation, metabolic health, your partner's semen analysis and ovarian reserve help you move forward without guesswork. There is no universal cutoff, so your timeline depends on your own picture.

mainEntity.name: Should I get an AMH test if I have PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: AMH is often part of the assessment in PCOS, but the result needs careful reading. PCOS commonly raises AMH, so a high value does not mean egg quality is good, and a lower value does not rule out pregnancy. Your doctor will read AMH alongside your cycle pattern, ultrasound findings and your partner's semen report before suggesting a next step.

mainEntity.name: Can PCOS and diabetes affect pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: They can. Women with PCOS have a higher risk of gestational diabetes and high blood pressure during pregnancy. Screening blood sugar and blood pressure before conception lets your doctor plan ahead, and good metabolic control before and during pregnancy supports a healthier outcome. It is worth raising this early.

mainEntity.name: Do I need IVF straight away after 30 with PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not. Many women with PCOS begin with ovulation induction and monitoring, and IUI may be considered in suitable cases. IVF comes into the picture when other factors make it more appropriate, such as tubal problems, a significant semen issue, age-related concerns or earlier treatment that did not lead to pregnancy.

mainEntity.name: Where can I get a PCOS fertility assessment in Bangalore?

acceptedAnswer.text: EVE Women and Fertility Clinic in Gunjur, Bangalore, offers fertility consultation, ovulation induction, follicle monitoring and IUI under Dr. Swati Shree. Bring previous blood test reports and ultrasound records to your first visit. For IVF, she guides treatment through partner fertility centres in Bangalore.

mainEntity.name: Can I get pregnant naturally with PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, some women do, especially when cycles are only mildly irregular or after lifestyle changes. Ovulation may be unpredictable, so tracking helps. If you have not conceived after 6 to 12 months, see a doctor, because treatment is effective and time is valuable.

mainEntity.name: Is weight loss necessary to get pregnant with PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is not necessary for everyone. When weight is raised, a 5 to 10 percent loss can restore ovulation and improve pregnancy outcomes. Lean women with PCOS benefit more from regular activity and a balanced diet. Dr. Swati advises based on your own picture.

mainEntity.name: Does PCOS increase miscarriage risk?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some studies show a slightly higher risk, linked to weight, insulin resistance and age. Good sugar control and a healthy weight lower it. Many women with PCOS have healthy pregnancies. Early care and monitoring help.

mainEntity.name: Is IVF always needed in PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Many women with PCOS conceive with ovulation induction or IUI. IVF is considered when these do not work, or when there is a tubal or male factor. Dr. Swati will not recommend IVF before simpler steps have been tried, unless your tests point that way.

mainEntity.name: Will PCOS affect my pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: PCOS raises the chance of gestational diabetes and high blood pressure in pregnancy. Early checks, healthy habits and regular antenatal care manage these well. Dr. Swati advises on a plan during pregnancy.

mainEntity.name: Can I get pregnant naturally if I have PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. PCOS does not automatically prevent natural pregnancy. The main difficulty is often irregular ovulation. If ovulation occurs and there are no significant problems involving the fallopian tubes, sperm or other reproductive factors, natural conception may be possible.

mainEntity.name: Which treatment is usually used first for PCOS-related ovulation problems?

acceptedAnswer.text: For women with PCOS who are not ovulating and have no other infertility factors, letrozole is recommended as the first-line pharmacological treatment for ovulation induction. It should be prescribed and monitored by a qualified doctor.

mainEntity.name: Does PCOS mean I need IVF?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. IVF is not automatically required for PCOS. Depending on the fertility assessment, treatment may involve natural conception, ovulation induction or IUI. IVF may be considered when other treatment has not worked or another fertility factor makes it appropriate.

mainEntity.name: Is IUI useful for women with PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: IUI can be considered in selected cases. The decision depends on factors such as ovulation, sperm quality, tubal status, age and previous treatment. During IUI, prepared sperm is placed into the uterus around the time of ovulation.

mainEntity.name: Can irregular periods mean I am not ovulating?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Very irregular or absent periods can indicate ovulatory dysfunction. However, the exact situation needs medical assessment. A fertility specialist may use menstrual history, blood tests or ultrasound to assess ovulation.

mainEntity.name: Should my partner have a semen analysis if I have PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, where applicable. Fertility problems can involve the woman, the man, both partners or sometimes no clearly identifiable factor. A semen analysis can help identify male-factor fertility problems before treatment is planned.

mainEntity.name: When should a woman with PCOS see a fertility specialist?

acceptedAnswer.text: Earlier assessment may be useful when periods are very irregular or absent. In general, evaluation is considered after 12 months of trying for women under 35 and after 6 months for women aged 35 or older. Known fertility concerns may justify earlier evaluation.

mainEntity.name: Where can I get fertility care for PCOS in East Bangalore?

acceptedAnswer.text: EVE Women and Fertility Clinic in Gunjur, Bangalore provides fertility assessment, ovulation induction, follicle monitoring and IUI within its documented ART Level 1 scope. Advanced IVF procedures are carried out through the clinic's documented partner fertility centres. Pasted text

@graph.headline: PCOS and IVF: When Is IVF Needed and When Is It Not?

mainEntity.name: Does PCOS always end in IVF?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not. Many women with PCOS are first checked for ovulation and may be offered induction or IUI. IVF is generally considered once those options have not led to pregnancy, or sooner if a factor such as blocked tubes or a significant male-factor problem is found. Your specialist will explain how those findings apply to you.

mainEntity.name: Why would a doctor skip IUI and suggest IVF?

acceptedAnswer.text: The usual reasons include blocked or damaged fallopian tubes, severely reduced sperm parameters, several monitored cycles without pregnancy, or conditions such as significant endometriosis. IUI places prepared sperm into the uterus, while IVF fertilises eggs in the laboratory. Your own tests and history will show which route makes sense.

mainEntity.name: Is IVF more effective than IUI for PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single answer, because results depend on age, ovulation, sperm quality, tubal health, ovarian reserve and the reason for infertility. Published figures are averages across many people, so they rarely describe one couple accurately. Ask your doctor what your own factors suggest for each option.

mainEntity.name: Is IVF risky for women with PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: IVF is widely used, but women with PCOS have a higher chance of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, since their ovaries can react strongly to stimulation medicines. Protocols are adjusted and monitored closely to lower that risk. Severe abdominal pain, rapid swelling, breathlessness or reduced urine after treatment needs prompt medical review.

mainEntity.name: Where can I get PCOS fertility care in East Bangalore?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dr. Swati Shree sees patients at EVE Women and Fertility Clinic in Gunjur, Bangalore. Ovulation induction, follicle monitoring and IUI are offered within the clinic's ART Level 1 scope, and IVF is guided through partner fertility centres in Bangalore. Patients from Whitefield, Varthur and Sarjapur Road can book a consultation to talk through their cycle history.

mainEntity.name: Can I conceive with PCOS if my periods are very irregular?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many women with very irregular periods do conceive. Infrequent periods suggest that ovulation is rare, which makes timing harder, but they do not rule out pregnancy. A specialist can confirm whether you are ovulating, check for other contributing factors and recommend a plan based on your history. Raising the question early can save you months of guessing.

mainEntity.name: Does PCOS always lead to IVF?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not. Many women begin with lifestyle changes and ovulation induction, and some move on to IUI once ovulation is achieved and other factors look favourable. IVF is considered when those options are unsuitable or have not worked, or when another factor makes it the better fit. The decision rests on a full assessment of both partners.

mainEntity.name: Where can I get a PCOS fertility evaluation in East Bangalore?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dr. Swati Shree at EVE Women and Fertility Clinic in Gunjur, Bangalore, sees women with PCOS, irregular periods and ovulation concerns. Consultations may include cycle review, hormone tests and follicular monitoring when needed. Advanced IVF procedures are carried out at partner fertility centres. A consultation is the most reliable way to learn what applies to your situation.

mainEntity.name: Are ovulation kits reliable for PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often they are not. The raised LH levels seen in PCOS can produce a positive result even when no egg is released, and a negative reading may miss rare ovulation. Kits can still offer some guidance, but they work best alongside a progesterone blood test or a follicular study. Ask your doctor how to read your results.

mainEntity.name: Can weight loss restore ovulation in PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: For some women who are overweight, gradual weight reduction improves ovulation and cycle regularity. Results vary, and women at a healthy weight can have ovulation problems too. Weight should never be blamed for infertility. Discuss any weight plan with your doctor, especially if you are planning pregnancy or taking medicines.

@graph.headline: PCOS and Pregnancy: Can You Conceive Naturally?

mainEntity.name: Can PCOS stop me from getting pregnant naturally?

acceptedAnswer.text: PCOS does not stop pregnancy by itself, but it often makes ovulation irregular, which reduces the number of fertile days. Plenty of women with PCOS conceive without medication once ovulation is confirmed. A fertility assessment can show whether ovulation, the tubes and semen results are working in your favour.

mainEntity.name: Why are my periods so irregular if I am trying to conceive?

acceptedAnswer.text: Irregular cycles usually mean ovulation is happening rarely, or not at all. Hormonal changes linked to PCOS can delay follicle maturity, so cycle length keeps shifting. A doctor can check hormone levels and arrange a scan to confirm what is going on. That is more reliable than counting days on a calendar.

mainEntity.name: If I have PCOS, will I need IVF?

acceptedAnswer.text: IVF is not usually the first step. Most women with PCOS are first evaluated for timed intercourse or ovulation induction, and some then move on to IUI. IVF is generally considered when those options have not led to pregnancy, or when another factor such as tubal disease is present. The right route is decided after a full assessment.

mainEntity.name: Should my partner have a semen test?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually, yes. Fertility difficulties can involve the woman, the man, both partners, or sometimes no obvious cause. A semen analysis looks at sperm count, movement and shape. Getting it done early means a male factor is not overlooked while ovulation treatment is underway, which can save time and frustration later.

mainEntity.name: How does IUI work for women with PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: IUI is considered in selected cases, usually once ovulation has been induced or is being closely monitored. Sperm is washed and prepared in the laboratory, then placed into the uterus close to the time of ovulation. Fertilisation still happens inside the body. Age, sperm quality, tube status and earlier treatment all shape whether it suits you.

mainEntity.name: Where can I get PCOS fertility care in East Bangalore?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dr. Swati Shree sees patients at EVE Women and Fertility Clinic in Gunjur, Bangalore. Care includes fertility assessment, counselling, ovulation induction, follicle monitoring and IUI. If IVF becomes the plan, egg retrieval and embryo transfer take place at partner fertility centres, and your care team explains that pathway step by step.

@graph.name: Positive Pregnancy Test After IVF: What Happens Next?
@graph.headline: Positive Pregnancy Test After IVF: What Happens Next?

mainEntity.name: Why is hCG repeated after a positive test?

acceptedAnswer.text: One result shows pregnancy, but a repeat test shows whether hCG is rising as expected. A healthy rise is reassuring. A slow rise or fall may need more tests or an early scan.

mainEntity.name: When will I have my first scan after IVF?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most clinics do the first ultrasound around 5 to 7 weeks of pregnancy. It confirms the pregnancy is in the uterus and shows the number of sacs. A heartbeat scan usually follows.

mainEntity.name: Is spotting normal in early IVF pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Light spotting can happen and does not always mean a problem. Still, inform your clinic about any bleeding. Heavy bleeding, clots or pain need prompt assessment.

mainEntity.name: How long do I need progesterone after IVF?

acceptedAnswer.text: It varies by clinic and type of transfer, but many women continue progesterone for several weeks. Your doctor will tell you when it is safe to stop. Do not stop on your own.

mainEntity.name: Is an IVF pregnancy high risk?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most IVF pregnancies progress like natural pregnancies. Some factors, such as twins, age or underlying conditions, may need closer monitoring. Your obstetrician will plan care based on your health.

mainEntity.name: When can I share the news?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is a personal choice. Many couples wait until after the heartbeat scan or the 12-week scan. Choose the time that feels right for you and your family.

@graph.headline: Pregnancy After 40: Fertility, Risks and Options

mainEntity.name: Can I get pregnant naturally after 40?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, some women do, especially in the early forties with good egg reserve and regular ovulation. The chance each month is lower than at younger ages, so early specialist advice is recommended.

mainEntity.name: Is pregnancy after 40 safe?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many women have healthy pregnancies after 40. Risks such as high blood pressure, diabetes and miscarriage are higher, so close antenatal care and early screening are important. Your obstetrician will plan monitoring.

mainEntity.name: Is IVF effective after 40?

acceptedAnswer.text: IVF can help some women over 40, but outcomes depend strongly on age and egg reserve. Your specialist will explain realistic expectations based on your tests rather than general figures.

mainEntity.name: What is PGT-A and should I consider it?

acceptedAnswer.text: PGT-A tests embryos for chromosome numbers before transfer. It may help select embryos in some women over 40, but it has limitations and costs. Discuss the benefits and drawbacks with your specialist.

mainEntity.name: When are donor eggs considered?

acceptedAnswer.text: Donor eggs may be discussed when egg reserve is very low, previous IVF cycles have not worked, or age significantly reduces the chance of success. Counselling helps couples make this personal decision.

mainEntity.name: What tests should I have before trying after 40?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common checks include AMH, thyroid, blood sugar, blood pressure, a pelvic scan and the partner's semen analysis. Starting folic acid and reviewing medicines are also important.

@graph.name: Pregnancy After IVF: Embryo Transfer & Early Pregnancy
@graph.headline: Pregnancy After IVF: Embryo Transfer & Early Pregnancy

mainEntity.name: How soon can I test for pregnancy after IVF embryo transfer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your fertility clinic will give you a specific date for pregnancy testing. Testing immediately after transfer is too early to provide a useful answer. Waiting until the recommended date allows enough time for implantation and hCG production. Very early testing can also be confusing when an hCG-containing medication was used during treatment.

mainEntity.name: What are the first signs of pregnancy after IVF?

acceptedAnswer.text: Early pregnancy may cause fatigue, breast tenderness, nausea, increased urination, mild cramping or spotting. However, these symptoms can also be caused by fertility medicines, particularly progesterone. Some women have very few symptoms. A pregnancy test and appropriate follow-up are more reliable than symptoms.

mainEntity.name: What happens after a positive IVF pregnancy test?

acceptedAnswer.text: After a positive test, your fertility team may repeat the hCG test and arrange an early ultrasound. The scan helps assess the location and development of the pregnancy. Your doctor will also review your medicines and explain the next stage of pregnancy care.

mainEntity.name: Can you feel implantation after embryo transfer?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no reliable symptom that confirms implantation. Mild cramping or spotting may occur, but these symptoms can have several causes. Some women experience no noticeable symptoms at all. Implantation is assessed indirectly through subsequent hCG testing and, later, ultrasound findings.

mainEntity.name: Can an ectopic pregnancy happen after IVF?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. IVF does not completely eliminate the possibility of an ectopic pregnancy. This is why early pregnancy monitoring includes attention to the location of the pregnancy. Severe or one-sided pelvic pain, bleeding, shoulder-tip pain, fainting or significant dizziness should receive prompt medical assessment.

mainEntity.name: Should I continue progesterone after a positive IVF test?

acceptedAnswer.text: Do not stop progesterone or another prescribed IVF medicine without speaking with your fertility doctor. The type and duration of hormonal support depend on the treatment protocol and individual circumstances. If you are unsure whether to continue a medicine, contact your fertility clinic for specific instructions.

mainEntity.name: Is early pregnancy monitoring different after frozen embryo transfer?

acceptedAnswer.text: The treatment used to prepare the uterus can differ between frozen embryo transfer cycles, but the main principles of early pregnancy monitoring remain similar. hCG testing and an ultrasound may be used to assess pregnancy development and location. Your doctor will determine the appropriate schedule.

mainEntity.name: Where can I get fertility and early pregnancy guidance in East Bangalore?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dr. Swati Shree provides fertility evaluation and counselling at EVE Women and Fertility Clinic in Gunjur, Bangalore. Advanced IVF laboratory procedures are performed through EVE's partner fertility centres, including Apollo Fertility and Motherhood Fertility, where Dr. Swati Shree is a visiting consultant. @graph.headline: Pregnancy With Endometriosis Without IVF: Is It Possible?

mainEntity.name: Can mild endometriosis stop pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mild endometriosis can reduce fertility slightly, but many women with it conceive naturally. If pregnancy does not happen within a reasonable time for your age, your doctor may suggest IUI or other options.

mainEntity.name: Does IUI work for endometriosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: IUI with ovulation support may help some women with mild endometriosis, open tubes and normal sperm. It is less suitable when tubes are damaged or the disease is advanced. Your test results guide the choice.

mainEntity.name: Should I have surgery before trying to conceive?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. Surgery may help when pain is significant or adhesions are suspected. For ovarian cysts, surgery can reduce egg reserve, so the decision is made carefully with a fertility specialist.

mainEntity.name: Can I take hormone tablets for pain while trying to conceive?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many hormonal treatments for endometriosis pain prevent ovulation, so they are usually stopped when you are trying to get pregnant. Your doctor can suggest other ways to manage pain during this time.

mainEntity.name: How long should I try naturally with endometriosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on your age and test results. Younger women with mild disease may try for a while, while women over 35 or with other factors may be advised to seek help sooner. Your specialist will guide you.

mainEntity.name: Does endometriosis come back after pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Symptoms often ease during pregnancy but may return after delivery or breastfeeding. Long-term care depends on your symptoms and future plans. Regular follow-up helps manage it well.

@graph.name: Recurrent Miscarriage: Causes, Tests & Treatment
@graph.headline: Recurrent Miscarriage: Causes, Tests & Treatment

mainEntity.name: How many miscarriages are considered recurrent pregnancy loss?

acceptedAnswer.text: The definition of recurrent pregnancy loss can vary between medical guidelines and clinical situations. Doctors consider not only the number of miscarriages but also when they occurred, previous ultrasound findings, genetic results and the couple's medical history. A fertility specialist can determine whether an evaluation is appropriate.

mainEntity.name: What is the most common cause of recurrent miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single cause that explains every case. Chromosomal abnormalities are an important cause of pregnancy loss, particularly early in pregnancy. Other possibilities include uterine abnormalities, antiphospholipid syndrome, endocrine conditions and genetic factors involving a parent. Some couples have no identifiable cause after evaluation.

mainEntity.name: What blood tests are done for recurrent miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Blood tests are selected according to the patient's history. They may include testing related to antiphospholipid syndrome, thyroid function and selected endocrine or metabolic conditions. Genetic testing may also be discussed in appropriate cases. A doctor should decide which tests are useful rather than ordering every available blood test.

mainEntity.name: Can thyroid problems cause recurrent miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Thyroid disorders can affect pregnancy, particularly when thyroid function is not appropriately managed. However, thyroid disease should not automatically be assumed to be the cause of recurrent miscarriage. A doctor can assess thyroid function and consider the result alongside the complete pregnancy and medical history.

mainEntity.name: Can recurrent miscarriage be treated?

acceptedAnswer.text: Treatment depends on the underlying cause. Depending on the findings, management may include treating an identified medical condition, addressing certain uterine abnormalities, managing antiphospholipid syndrome or providing genetic counselling. When no cause is identified, preconception planning and appropriate monitoring during a future pregnancy may still be useful.

mainEntity.name: Is IVF recommended for recurrent miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: IVF is not automatically recommended after recurrent miscarriage. It may be considered when there is another fertility indication or when particular genetic circumstances make assisted reproduction relevant. Embryo genetic testing may be discussed in selected cases, but IVF cannot guarantee that a future pregnancy will continue normally.

mainEntity.name: Can I have a healthy pregnancy after recurrent miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, a healthy future pregnancy can be possible after recurrent pregnancy loss. The appropriate care depends on factors such as age, medical history, previous pregnancy findings and test results. No treatment can guarantee a particular outcome, but identifying a treatable cause and planning early pregnancy care can help guide management.

mainEntity.name: Where can recurrent miscarriage be evaluated in Bangalore?

acceptedAnswer.text: Recurrent pregnancy loss can be assessed by a gynecologist or fertility specialist with experience in reproductive medicine. Dr. Swati Shree provides fertility evaluation at EVE Women and Fertility Clinic in Gunjur, Bangalore, where the assessment can be tailored to the individual's previous pregnancy history and medical findings.

@graph.name: When Is Miscarriage Called Recurrent Pregnancy Loss?
@graph.headline: When Is Miscarriage Called Recurrent Pregnancy Loss?

mainEntity.name: How many miscarriages before testing is recommended?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many specialists now recommend evaluation after two pregnancy losses, rather than waiting for three. Testing may be advised after one loss in women over 35 or with other fertility concerns.

mainEntity.name: Is recurrent miscarriage caused by something I did?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not. Most miscarriages are due to chromosomal problems in the embryo, which are not caused by anything the woman did. Normal activity, work and intercourse do not cause miscarriage.

mainEntity.name: Can I have a healthy pregnancy after recurrent miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Many couples go on to have a healthy pregnancy, even when no cause is found. Close monitoring and support in the next pregnancy can be helpful.

mainEntity.name: Do men need to be tested after recurrent miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, both partners may be offered blood tests to check chromosomes. Sperm DNA testing may be discussed in selected cases. Your specialist will decide what is useful.

mainEntity.name: Does age affect the risk of miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The risk of miscarriage rises with the woman's age, mainly because of chromosomal changes in eggs. This is why women over 35 may be evaluated sooner.

mainEntity.name: Should I try again soon after a miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on your physical and emotional readiness and your doctor's advice. Many women can try again after their next normal period. If you have had recurrent losses, evaluation first is often helpful.

@graph.headline: Semen Analysis Explained: Count, Motility and Morphology

mainEntity.name: What is a normal sperm count?

acceptedAnswer.text: Labs use reference values, often based on World Health Organization standards, to decide what is within the expected range. Your report will show these values. A count slightly below the range does not always mean infertility.

mainEntity.name: Can I collect a semen sample at home?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some labs allow home collection if the sample reaches them within the advised time and is kept at body temperature. Others prefer collection on site. Ask the lab for clear instructions before you start.

mainEntity.name: What does low motility mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: Low motility means fewer sperm are moving forward well. This can make it harder for sperm to reach the egg. Treatment depends on the cause and severity, and may include IUI or IVF with ICSI.

mainEntity.name: Is low morphology a serious problem?

acceptedAnswer.text: Morphology is judged by strict criteria, so many fertile men have a low percentage of normal forms. On its own, it may have limited impact. Doctors look at all values together.

mainEntity.name: How long does a semen analysis take?

acceptedAnswer.text: The test is usually completed on the same day, and results are often available within a day or two. Some advanced tests, such as DNA fragmentation, may take longer.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if my semen analysis is abnormal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Do not panic. Ask your doctor to repeat the test after a few weeks. If it is still abnormal, further tests may be advised. Many problems can be treated or worked around with assisted reproduction.

@graph.headline: Tests After Recurrent Miscarriage: What Is Checked

mainEntity.name: Do I need every test after recurrent miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Tests are chosen based on your history, age, timing of losses and previous results. Your specialist will recommend tests that are useful for your situation and avoid those with limited value.

mainEntity.name: What is antiphospholipid syndrome?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is an immune condition where antibodies increase the risk of blood clots, which can affect the placenta. It is a treatable cause of recurrent miscarriage. Diagnosis needs positive tests on two occasions about 12 weeks apart.

mainEntity.name: Why test the uterus after miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Problems such as a uterine septum, fibroids or polyps can interfere with implantation or pregnancy growth. Many of these can be treated with minor surgery like hysteroscopy.

mainEntity.name: What is a parental karyotype?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is a blood test that checks the chromosomes of both partners. In a small number of couples, one partner carries a balanced chromosome change that can lead to pregnancy loss. Genetic counselling helps plan next steps.

mainEntity.name: Can thyroid problems cause miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Untreated thyroid problems are linked with a higher risk of pregnancy loss. Testing TSH and treating abnormal levels before and during pregnancy is a simple and important step.

mainEntity.name: Should pregnancy tissue be tested after a miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: If possible, testing tissue from a future loss can show whether chromosome problems were the cause. This can help guide further evaluation. Ask your doctor whether it can be arranged.

mainEntity.name: Can hypothyroidism prevent pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hypothyroidism can disturb ovulation and cycles and make conception harder, but with treatment many women conceive. Controlling thyroid levels before pregnancy improves fertility and pregnancy outcomes.

mainEntity.name: What TSH level is best for pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many specialists aim for a lower TSH range when trying to conceive, but the exact target is individual. Your doctor will set the right range for you and monitor it regularly.

mainEntity.name: Should I take thyroid medicine during pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you have hypothyroidism, treatment is important and generally continued during pregnancy, often at a higher dose. Do not stop or change your medicine without your doctor's advice.

mainEntity.name: Can thyroid antibodies cause miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Thyroid antibodies are linked with a higher risk of miscarriage in some women, even with normal hormone levels. Your doctor may monitor your thyroid more closely during pregnancy.

mainEntity.name: Do both partners need thyroid tests?

acceptedAnswer.text: Thyroid testing is mainly advised for women, but men with symptoms or abnormal semen analysis may also be tested. Your fertility specialist will decide which tests are needed.

@graph.name: Unexplained Infertility: When Fertility Tests Are Normal
@graph.headline: Unexplained Infertility: When Fertility Tests Are Normal

mainEntity.name: What does unexplained infertility mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: It means standard fertility tests for both partners are normal, yet pregnancy has not occurred after the recommended time of trying. A specific cause has not been identified by routine tests.

mainEntity.name: Can couples with unexplained infertility get pregnant naturally?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, some couples conceive naturally, especially when younger and with a shorter duration of trying. Others benefit from treatment such as IUI or IVF.

mainEntity.name: Is IUI or IVF better for unexplained infertility?

acceptedAnswer.text: IUI with ovulation induction may be tried first in some couples, while IVF is often recommended for older women or after unsuccessful IUI. Your specialist will advise based on your situation.

mainEntity.name: What causes unexplained infertility?

acceptedAnswer.text: Possible hidden causes include egg or sperm quality issues, mild endometriosis, fertilisation problems and implantation difficulties that routine tests cannot detect.

mainEntity.name: Should we do more tests for unexplained infertility?

acceptedAnswer.text: Additional tests may sometimes be considered, but many couples move to treatment rather than extensive testing. Your specialist will discuss what is useful.

@graph.headline: What to Do After IUI: Precautions, Symptoms and Pregnancy

mainEntity.name: Can I go to work after IUI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Most women return to work the same day or the next. Avoid very heavy lifting or intense exercise for a few days if your doctor advises it.

mainEntity.name: Is spotting after IUI normal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Light spotting can happen from the catheter or from progesterone. It does not confirm or rule out pregnancy. Tell your clinic about any bleeding, and call urgently if it is heavy or comes with pain.

mainEntity.name: When can I have intercourse after IUI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your doctor will advise. Many clinics say it is safe after a short interval, but follow your own instructions.

mainEntity.name: How soon can I take a pregnancy test after IUI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most clinics suggest about 14 days after IUI. Testing earlier may give a false result, especially if you had a trigger injection.

mainEntity.name: What symptoms mean I should call the doctor?

acceptedAnswer.text: Heavy bleeding, severe or one-sided pain, fever, marked bloating with rapid weight gain, breathlessness, fainting or very little urine need prompt medical attention.

@graph.name: When Is IVF Recommended? Key Situations Explained
@graph.headline: When Is IVF Recommended? Key Situations Explained

mainEntity.name: How many IUI cycles should be tried before IVF is suggested?

acceptedAnswer.text: No fixed number suits everyone. The decision depends on your age, the diagnosis, how your ovaries responded and how many cycles have already been done. Women over 35, or those with a clear reason to act sooner, are often advised to move on earlier. Ask your doctor to walk you through the reasoning behind the advice, so the plan makes sense to you.

mainEntity.name: Can IVF help if both fallopian tubes are blocked?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The egg is fertilised in the laboratory and the embryo is placed directly into the uterus, so the tubes are bypassed. Blocked tubes are one of the most common reasons for suggesting IVF. Some tube problems, such as a fluid-filled tube, may need treatment before transfer. Your specialist will review your imaging before planning the cycle.

mainEntity.name: Does a low AMH mean IVF is always needed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. A low AMH does not automatically call for IVF, and it does not mean pregnancy is impossible. Some couples with low AMH conceive naturally or with IUI, particularly when other factors are favourable. AMH helps estimate how many eggs may be collected, so it informs the treatment choice alongside everything else. A personal consultation gives the clearest picture.

mainEntity.name: Is IVF recommended for men with a low sperm count?

acceptedAnswer.text: It may be, when sperm problems are severe, because ICSI can fertilise an egg using a single sperm. Milder male factor issues often respond to IUI. A semen analysis is usually among the first tests, since the report helps decide between IUI, IVF and ICSI. Stopping smoking and cutting back on alcohol may support sperm quality. A specialist can explain what applies to you.

mainEntity.name: Where can I get a fertility evaluation for IVF in East Bangalore?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can book a fertility consultation with Dr. Swati Shree at EVE Women and Fertility Clinic in Gunjur, Bangalore, which is convenient from Varthur, Whitefield, Sarjapur Road and Bellandur. She reviews your reports at EVE and, if IVF is needed, guides treatment through partner fertility centres in Bangalore. Having one specialist oversee your care from start to finish can make the process easier to follow.

citation: ASRM Practice Committee, Definition of infertility (2023)

mainEntity.name: How long should I try before seeing a doctor?

acceptedAnswer.text: Twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse for most couples, and six months if the woman is 35 or older. Go sooner if your periods are very irregular, you have a known condition, or you have had miscarriages. An early visit is allowed whatever your worry.

mainEntity.name: Do I have to start IVF if I see a fertility doctor?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The first visit is for evaluation. Many couples conceive with simple steps such as treating a thyroid problem, ovulation tracking or medicine for ovulation. IVF is advised only when it fits your situation. Dr. Swati does not default to it.

mainEntity.name: Should my husband or partner come too?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if possible. A male factor contributes to about half of couples' infertility, and a semen analysis is simple. Coming together saves time and gives a complete picture. If your partner cannot come, you can start, and he can join later.

mainEntity.name: Is it too early to see a doctor if I am in my twenties?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not if you have concerns. If you are under 35 and healthy, the 12-month rule applies. If you have irregular periods or a medical condition, there is no need to wait. A planning visit before you try can also help.

mainEntity.name: I want to delay pregnancy. Should I see a fertility doctor?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can help. A check of AMH and antral follicle count, plus a talk about egg freezing, gives you information. Age matters most, and the earlier you ask, the more options you have. Dr. Swati explains what is realistic, without pressure.

@graph.headline: Why Both Partners Need Fertility Evaluation

mainEntity.name: Why should the man be tested if the woman has irregular periods?

acceptedAnswer.text: Even if the woman has a known issue, the man may also have a sperm problem. Treating only one partner may not work. A semen analysis is simple and ensures nothing is missed.

mainEntity.name: Is male infertility common?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Male factors contribute in many couples who struggle to conceive, either alone or along with female factors. Testing both partners is the standard approach recommended by fertility specialists.

mainEntity.name: What is the first test for men?

acceptedAnswer.text: A semen analysis is the first test. It checks sperm count, movement and shape. It is quick, painless and gives important information for planning treatment.

mainEntity.name: Can both partners be tested on the same visit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Many clinics arrange the woman's scan and blood tests and the man's semen analysis around the same visit. This speeds up the process and allows results to be reviewed together.

mainEntity.name: What if both partners have normal tests?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is called unexplained infertility. It does not mean nothing can be done. Options may include timed intercourse, IUI or IVF, depending on age and how long the couple has been trying.

mainEntity.name: How can couples support each other through testing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Attend appointments together, share information openly and avoid blaming each other. Counselling and support groups can also help couples cope with the emotional side of fertility evaluation.

mainEntity.name: Can I have a consultation without travelling?

acceptedAnswer.text: At present, EVE focuses on in-person consultations, because fertility care needs an examination and scans. Reports can often be shared in advance so that the visit is more useful.

mainEntity.name: How many days should I plan for a first visit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most outstation couples plan two to three days. The consultation, scan and blood tests can often be done on the first day. A tubal test or a semen analysis may need a different day, depending on your cycle.

mainEntity.name: Can local scans be used for follicle tracking?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often, yes. Follicle tracking during a cycle can be done at a trusted local centre. You share the reports with Dr. Swati, who adjusts your plan. Procedures at the time of ovulation or egg collection need a visit to Bangalore.

mainEntity.name: Can I get IVF done in Bangalore if I live in another state?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, patients from other states can have IVF in Bangalore, within the ART Act's rules on eligibility and consent. The plan and the laboratory steps are explained at your first visit, and each cycle is timed with you.

mainEntity.name: Is there anywhere to stay nearby?

acceptedAnswer.text: Gunjur, Varthur and Whitefield have many hotels and service apartments. We can suggest the area to stay in, but we do not recommend or partner with any particular hotel.

mainEntity.name: What should I do first if I think I have a gynaecological condition?

acceptedAnswer.text: Note your symptoms, the dates of your last few periods, and any medicines you take. Bring past reports and scans. Book a consultation. Dr. Swati examines you, decides which tests are needed, and explains the diagnosis before any treatment begins.

mainEntity.name: Can I have more than one condition at once?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and this is common. PCOS and thyroid disease occur together often. Endometriosis, adenomyosis and fibroids can coexist. Dr. Swati looks at the whole picture, so that treating one does not worsen another.

mainEntity.name: Which symptoms need attention straight away?

acceptedAnswer.text: Very heavy bleeding that soaks through a pad every hour, sudden severe pelvic pain, fainting, fever with pelvic pain, or bleeding with pain in early pregnancy need urgent care. Call 108 or 112, or go to the nearest hospital emergency.

mainEntity.name: Do all conditions affect fertility?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Many conditions, such as simple fibroids or mild menstrual problems, do not stop you getting pregnant. Others, such as untreated PCOS, endometriosis or blocked tubes, can. A fertility evaluation shows whether your condition matters for conception.

mainEntity.name: What causes adenomyosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: The cause is not known. It may relate to uterine surgery or pregnancy, hormones, or how the lining invades the muscle. It is not caused by anything you did and is not infectious. Treatment aims at controlling symptoms and, when wanted, supporting pregnancy.

mainEntity.name: Can adenomyosis be cured?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hysterectomy ends adenomyosis, but it is only for women who have completed their families. Otherwise, symptoms can be controlled with medicine, a hormonal IUD or procedures, and they usually ease after menopause. Dr. Swati plans treatment around your goals.

mainEntity.name: Can I get pregnant with adenomyosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many women do. Adenomyosis can lower the chance of implantation and raise the risk of miscarriage, so some need fertility treatment. Dr. Swati evaluates other causes too, and advises early scans and closer follow-up once you are pregnant.

mainEntity.name: How is adenomyosis different from endometriosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: In adenomyosis, lining-type tissue grows into the muscle wall of the uterus. In endometriosis, it grows outside the uterus, such as on the ovaries or pelvic lining. They can occur together, and both cause painful periods.

mainEntity.name: Does adenomyosis need surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. Many women are managed with medicine or a hormonal IUD. Surgery is considered when symptoms persist, or when fertility goals require it. Dr. Swati explains the options, benefits and risks.

mainEntity.name: Does adenomyosis go away after menopause?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually the symptoms ease after menopause, because the condition depends on hormones. Heavy bleeding or new pain after menopause is not expected and should be checked.

mainEntity.name: What causes endometriosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: The cause is not fully known. Possible factors include menstrual blood flowing backwards, immune and hormonal factors, and genetics. It is not caused by anything you did, and it is not contagious. It is a chronic condition that can be managed.

mainEntity.name: Is painful periods normal or is it endometriosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mild cramps are common. Pain that stops you from going to work or school, needs strong painkillers, or comes with heavy bleeding or pain during sex is not something to ignore. It may be endometriosis, adenomyosis or another condition. A check is worthwhile.

mainEntity.name: Can I get pregnant with endometriosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many women do, naturally or with treatment. Endometriosis can reduce fertility, especially when tubes are damaged or reserve is low. Dr. Swati checks your tubes, reserve and your partner's semen, then explains whether to try naturally, use IUI, or move to IVF.

mainEntity.name: Do I need surgery for endometriosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. Many women are managed with medicine. Surgery is considered for severe pain that does not improve, large endometriomas, deep disease, or specific fertility reasons. Dr. Swati explains benefits and risks, including the effect of ovarian surgery on egg reserve.

mainEntity.name: Does endometriosis come back after treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can. Hormonal treatment after surgery lowers the chance. Long-term treatment is common unless you plan pregnancy. Pregnancy often brings relief while it lasts, but it is not a treatment. Regular review keeps symptoms in control.

mainEntity.name: Does endometriosis increase the risk of cancer?

acceptedAnswer.text: The risk of ovarian cancer is slightly higher in some types, but the overall chance remains low. Most women with endometriosis do not develop cancer. Follow-up and scanning of cysts help, and Dr. Swati advises when further tests are needed.

mainEntity.name: What is the most common cause of female infertility?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ovulation problems are among the most common, with PCOS the most common cause. Tubal damage and endometriosis are also frequent, and age-related decline is a key factor after 35. Often more than one factor is present, so a full evaluation matters.

mainEntity.name: Can a woman be infertile with regular periods?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Regular periods suggest ovulation is likely, but they do not show whether tubes are open, the uterus is healthy, or the eggs are of good quality. A fertility evaluation looks at these.

mainEntity.name: Does age affect fertility in women?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Fertility declines gradually from the late twenties, and more steeply after 35, because egg number and quality fall. The chance of miscarriage also rises with age. This is why older women are advised to seek help after 6 months of trying.

mainEntity.name: Can blocked fallopian tubes be treated?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some can, with surgery, when damage is mild. For many women with blocked tubes, IVF is advised because it bypasses the tubes. If one tube is open, timed attempts or IUI may still work. Dr. Swati explains which suits your findings.

mainEntity.name: Does genital tuberculosis cause infertility?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can. Genital TB may damage the tubes and uterine lining, and it can be present without obvious symptoms. It is considered when tests suggest it, especially with tubal damage or a thin lining. It is treatable with the right medicines.

mainEntity.name: Can lifestyle changes improve female fertility?

acceptedAnswer.text: They can help. Quitting smoking, limiting alcohol, achieving a healthy weight, and managing thyroid and diabetes support ovulation and general fertility. They do not replace treatment for blocked tubes or very low reserve, but improving them gives treatment a better chance.

mainEntity.name: Are fibroids cancer?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Fibroids are non-cancerous growths of muscle in the uterus. A cancerous change in a fibroid is very rare. Rapid growth after menopause, or unusual features on a scan, are reasons for closer evaluation.

mainEntity.name: Do fibroids stop me getting pregnant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not usually. Most women with fibroids conceive. Fibroids that distort the uterine cavity, especially submucosal fibroids, can reduce implantation and raise miscarriage risk. Dr. Swati identifies whether your fibroids matter, and removal is advised only when it is likely to help.

mainEntity.name: Do all fibroids need treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Fibroids without symptoms and not affecting fertility can be watched with regular review. Treatment is advised for heavy bleeding, anaemia, pressure symptoms, pain, or fertility problems linked to the fibroid.

mainEntity.name: Can fibroids be treated without surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often. Medicines can reduce bleeding and pain, and a hormonal IUD helps heavy periods in many women. Medicines do not remove fibroids, but they can control symptoms. Surgery is considered when symptoms persist or the fibroid affects fertility.

mainEntity.name: Will fibroids come back after surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: They can. Removal of a fibroid does not stop new ones forming, especially in younger women with many fibroids. Hysterectomy ends the risk, but is only for women who have completed their families. Dr. Swati discusses the chance of recurrence.

mainEntity.name: Do fibroids shrink after menopause?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually, yes, because they depend on estrogen. Fibroids tend to shrink after menopause, and symptoms ease. Growth after menopause, or bleeding, is not expected and should be checked.

mainEntity.name: At what age does menopause start in India?

acceptedAnswer.text: Studies suggest an average age of about 46 to 47 years among Indian women, a few years earlier than in many Western countries. Perimenopause can begin earlier, even in the late thirties or early forties. Early menopause is before 45, and premature menopause before 40.

mainEntity.name: What are the first signs of perimenopause?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often, periods become irregular, shorter or longer, lighter or heavier. Hot flushes, night sweats, poor sleep, mood changes, and vaginal dryness may follow. Symptoms can be confused with thyroid problems, so a check is worth it if you are unsure.

mainEntity.name: Is hormone therapy safe?

acceptedAnswer.text: For many healthy women under 60, or within 10 years of menopause, hormone therapy is safe and the most effective treatment for hot flushes. Risks depend on your age, history and type of therapy. It is not suitable for everyone. Dr. Swati reviews your risks and explains the choices.

mainEntity.name: Can I get pregnant during perimenopause?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Ovulation becomes unpredictable, but it still occurs, so pregnancy is possible until menopause is confirmed. If you do not want to conceive, continue contraception until a doctor advises it is safe to stop.

mainEntity.name: How can I protect my bones and heart after menopause?

acceptedAnswer.text: Exercise regularly, including weight-bearing and strength work. Eat enough calcium, protein and vitamin D, and avoid smoking and heavy alcohol. Control blood pressure, sugar and cholesterol. A bone density test may be advised, and treatment started if bone loss is significant.

mainEntity.name: Is bleeding after menopause normal?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Any bleeding after 12 months without periods needs a check, usually a pelvic ultrasound and sometimes a biopsy. Most causes are benign, such as thin lining or polyps, but a few are serious, and early evaluation matters.

mainEntity.name: What is a normal period?

acceptedAnswer.text: In adults, cycles usually come every 21 to 35 days, and last up to 8 days, with a flow that does not stop you from living normally. Cycles vary a little each month. Teenagers can have longer, more irregular cycles in the first two years.

mainEntity.name: Why are my periods irregular?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common causes are PCOS, thyroid problems, high prolactin, stress, weight change, intense exercise, breastfeeding and approaching menopause. Pregnancy should always be ruled out. A history, a scan and a few blood tests usually find the cause.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my bleeding is too heavy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Heavy bleeding means soaking through a pad every hour or two, passing large clots, bleeding that lasts over 8 days, or feeling tired, dizzy or breathless. If periods affect work or sleep, or you may be anaemic, see a doctor.

mainEntity.name: Can heavy periods be treated without surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often, yes. Non-hormonal tablets that reduce bleeding, hormonal pills and a hormonal IUD are effective for many women. Treatment depends on the cause. Fibroids, polyps and adenomyosis may need procedures. Dr. Swati explains all options.

mainEntity.name: Does an irregular cycle affect fertility?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if it means you ovulate irregularly or not at all. Irregular periods are a common sign of PCOS or thyroid problems, both treatable. A fertility evaluation and follicular monitoring show whether you ovulate and when.

mainEntity.name: I missed my period. Should I worry?

acceptedAnswer.text: First do a pregnancy test. If it is negative and you miss three periods in a row, or are late repeatedly, see a doctor. Causes include stress, weight change, PCOS, thyroid problems and early menopause. They are usually treatable.

mainEntity.name: Is PCOS the same as PCOD?

acceptedAnswer.text: In everyday use, PCOD and PCOS describe the same condition: ovaries with many small follicles, irregular ovulation and hormone changes. PCOS is the medical term. What matters is not the name but your symptoms, the tests and a plan matched to your goals.

mainEntity.name: Can I get pregnant with PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Many women with PCOS conceive, often with lifestyle changes and ovulation-inducing medicine, with monitoring. Some need IUI or IVF. PCOS makes ovulation irregular, but it does not mean you cannot become pregnant. Dr. Swati plans treatment after checking your tubes and partner's semen.

mainEntity.name: Does PCOS go away?

acceptedAnswer.text: PCOS does not go away, but it can be managed. Symptoms such as irregular periods and acne often improve with treatment and lifestyle changes, and ovulation can become regular. Long-term checks on sugar, cholesterol and blood pressure remain important, even when you feel well.

mainEntity.name: Do I have to lose weight to treat PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not everyone needs to. If weight is raised, losing 5 to 10 percent can improve cycles, ovulation and sugar control. Lean women with PCOS benefit from activity, sleep and a balanced diet. Dr. Swati sets realistic, kind goals without blame.

mainEntity.name: Which diet helps in PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single PCOS diet. A balanced diet with whole grains, pulses, vegetables, healthy fats and adequate protein, with fewer sweet drinks and refined foods, helps most women. Extreme diets are not advised. A food plan that suits your culture, budget and routine works best.

mainEntity.name: Can PCOS cause diabetes?

acceptedAnswer.text: PCOS raises the risk of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Regular checks on blood sugar, and lifestyle measures, lower the risk. If you plan pregnancy, sugar and thyroid levels are checked first, since both affect fertility and pregnancy.

mainEntity.name: Are birth control pills the only treatment for irregular periods in PCOS?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Pills are one option when pregnancy is not wanted, and they regulate periods and reduce acne. Other options include progestins, lifestyle changes, and medicine for insulin resistance. If you want to conceive, ovulation induction is used instead. Dr. Swati matches treatment to your goals.

mainEntity.name: How many miscarriages count as recurrent?

acceptedAnswer.text: The ESHRE 2022 guideline defines recurrent pregnancy loss as two or more pregnancy losses. Earlier definitions required three. Doctors now start the evaluation after two, so that treatable causes are found sooner.

mainEntity.name: Is it my fault?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Most miscarriages happen because the embryo has a chromosome error, which is chance and not caused by work, stress, exercise, a fall, or anything you did. Please be kind to yourself. A medical evaluation looks for causes that can be treated.

mainEntity.name: Will I be able to carry a pregnancy to term?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many couples with recurrent loss do, including those with no cause found. The chance depends on age, the number of earlier losses and any cause found. Dr. Swati reviews your history and explains your outlook honestly, without false promises.

mainEntity.name: What tests should I have after two miscarriages?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually antiphospholipid antibodies, a pelvic ultrasound or hysteroscopy, thyroid and blood sugar tests, prolactin and sometimes karyotyping of both partners. Dr. Swati chooses based on your history. Tests that guidelines do not support are not recommended.

mainEntity.name: Can I take any treatment during my next pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Treatment depends on the cause. In confirmed APS, aspirin and heparin help. For some women with bleeding and earlier loss, progesterone may be considered. For unexplained loss, supportive care and early scans are advised. Dr. Swati explains the evidence for any option.

mainEntity.name: When can I try again after a miscarriage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many couples can try again after one normal period, once physical and emotional recovery allow. If you have had two or more losses, getting evaluated first is wise. Dr. Swati can guide the timing and the early scan.

@graph.name: Low AMH and Thin Endometrium Care in Bangalore | EVE
Diminished ovarian reserve and thin endometrium

mainEntity.name: What is a normal AMH level?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single normal level. AMH falls with age, and values are compared with the typical range for your age and the laboratory. Very low values suggest reduced reserve, and very high values are seen in PCOS. Dr. Swati reads your AMH with your age, scan and history.

mainEntity.name: Does low AMH mean I cannot get pregnant?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. AMH reflects egg number, not quality, and women with low AMH can conceive naturally. It may mean that fewer eggs respond to stimulation, and that time is shorter. Acting earlier matters. Dr. Swati advises on options such as timed attempts, IUI or IVF.

mainEntity.name: Can I increase my AMH?

acceptedAnswer.text: AMH cannot be increased in any proven way, since it reflects eggs already present. Supplements and treatments sold for this purpose have little evidence. Healthy habits, such as stopping smoking, support general health. If you plan pregnancy, an early evaluation helps more.

mainEntity.name: What is a thin endometrium, and can it be treated?

acceptedAnswer.text: A thin endometrium is a lining that is thinner than needed for implantation, often under about 7 mm. Causes include low estrogen, scarring and infection. Treating the cause, estrogen support, and sometimes freezing embryos for a better prepared transfer can help.

mainEntity.name: Can I freeze eggs if my reserve is low?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sometimes. With low reserve, fewer eggs are collected in each cycle, and more than one cycle may be needed. Egg freezing may still be worth discussing, especially if you are young, but the benefit is less certain. Dr. Swati gives a realistic view.

mainEntity.name: Does a thin lining always cause implantation failure?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Pregnancies can occur with a thin lining, though the chance is lower. A thin lining is one factor among several. Dr. Swati checks for treatable causes, such as adhesions or infection, before advising a plan.

Thyroid disorders in women planning pregnancy

mainEntity.name: Can hypothyroidism cause infertility?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. An underactive thyroid can cause irregular ovulation, heavy or irregular periods, and a higher risk of miscarriage. Most women conceive once thyroid levels are corrected with medicine. It is one of the simplest causes of infertility to test for and treat.

mainEntity.name: What TSH level is right when trying to conceive?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many guidelines aim for a TSH below about 2.5 mIU/L when planning pregnancy, though targets vary slightly. Dr. Swati sets a target for you, based on your tests and history, and adjusts your dose to reach it.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to change my thyroid dose in pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often, yes. Pregnancy raises the need for thyroid hormone, and many women need a higher dose, often by about 25 to 30 percent. Contact your doctor as soon as you have a positive test, and do not adjust the dose on your own.

mainEntity.name: Does thyroid medicine harm the baby?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Thyroid hormone replacement is safe in pregnancy, and untreated hypothyroidism is far more harmful. Overactive thyroid needs particular care in medicine choice. Dr. Swati explains your plan and coordinates with an endocrinologist when needed.

mainEntity.name: Should I get thyroid antibodies tested?

acceptedAnswer.text: They may be useful if you have had miscarriages, or if TSH is borderline. Having antibodies increases the chance of thyroid problems later, so monitoring is advised. Treating antibodies alone is not clearly proven to help. Dr. Swati decides whether testing is useful for you.

mainEntity.name: Can thyroid problems cause irregular periods?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Both underactive and overactive thyroid can change cycle length and flow. A thyroid test is part of the first check for irregular periods. See the Menstrual disorders and PCOS pages.

mainEntity.name: What kind of doctor is Dr. Swati Shree?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dr. Swati Shree is an obstetrician and gynaecologist who specialises in reproductive medicine. She holds a DNB in obstetrics and gynaecology, a fellowship in reproductive medicine from KJK Hospital in Trivandrum, and an MRCOG from the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists in the UK. She looks after fertility problems and women's health conditions.

mainEntity.name: What does MRCOG mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: MRCOG stands for Member of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists. It is a UK postgraduate qualification earned by passing demanding written and clinical examinations in obstetrics and gynaecology. It does not indicate a treatment outcome, but it shows training to an international standard.

mainEntity.name: Which languages does Dr. Swati speak?

acceptedAnswer.text: English, Hindi and Kannada. You can speak in the language you are most comfortable with, and she will explain your reports and plan in the same language.

mainEntity.name: Where does Dr. Swati see patients?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dr. Swati sees patients at EVE Women and Fertility Clinic, 1st Floor, LG Complex Towers, Gunjur, Bangalore 560087. Call 72049 21212 or 72049 21516 to book. She previously worked as a consultant at associated fertility centres.

mainEntity.name: Do I see Dr. Swati herself at every visit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. EVE is a founder-led clinic, and Dr. Swati sees every patient herself. Scans and tests may be done by trained staff under her supervision, but the consultation, the plan and the decisions are hers and yours.

mainEntity.name: How can I check Dr. Swati's registration?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dr. Swati is registered with the Karnataka Medical Council, registration number DLH20090000353KTK. You can verify registered doctors through the National Medical Commission's Indian Medical Register, or by contacting the Karnataka Medical Council.

mainEntity.name: When should I see a fertility specialist?

acceptedAnswer.text: See a specialist if you have not conceived after 12 months of trying, or after 6 months if the woman is 35 or older. See one sooner if periods are very irregular or absent, you have known endometriosis, fibroids or tubal problems, you have had two or more miscarriages, or the male partner has a known semen problem.

mainEntity.name: Do I need IVF to get pregnant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Many couples conceive with ovulation tracking, treatment of a hormone problem, or IUI. IVF is usually advised when the tubes are blocked, sperm counts are very low, other treatments have not worked, or age and ovarian reserve leave little time. Dr. Swati recommends the starting point after your evaluation.

mainEntity.name: Does EVE offer IVF?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dr. Swati plans and guides IVF with you at EVE. The laboratory procedures, such as egg collection, embryo culture and embryo transfer, are carried out at associated ART centres that are registered under Indian law.

mainEntity.name: Can my partner come to the visit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and we encourage it. Fertility involves both partners, and the male partner's semen analysis is one of the first tests. Partners are welcome in the consultation room, and you can also come alone if you prefer.

mainEntity.name: Do you tell the sex of the baby on a scan?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Disclosing or testing for the sex of the baby is prohibited by Indian law, and we never do it. A scan at EVE is for checking location, growth and the heartbeat.

mainEntity.name: Do I need an appointment?

acceptedAnswer.text: An appointment is recommended, because consultations are unhurried and slots are planned. Call 72049 21212, use the form or message on WhatsApp. If you must walk in, we will fit you in as soon as we can.

mainEntity.name: How long is a first consultation?

acceptedAnswer.text: The first consultation is the longest visit, because Dr. Swati takes a complete history. Plan for enough time, and bring your partner if you can.

mainEntity.name: What if my periods start on the day of my appointment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Come anyway for the consultation. Some tests, such as an HSG, need the days just after your period, and others are timed later in the cycle. Tell the front desk when you book, and Dr. Swati plans around your cycle.

mainEntity.name: Can I bring someone with me?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Your partner, a family member or a friend is welcome in the consultation. For an examination or scan, you may choose who stays. A female attendant is available.

mainEntity.name: Is the clinic open on Sundays and holidays?

acceptedAnswer.text: Please call before you travel on a holiday.

mainEntity.name: Will I have to undress for the first visit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. The first visit is mainly a conversation. If an examination or transvaginal scan is needed, it is explained first and done only with your consent, in privacy. You can ask for a pause at any point.

mainEntity.name: Which service is right for me?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you are not sure, book a consultation. Dr. Swati reviews your history first and then decides which tests or services help. You do not need to know the right service in advance, and you are not committing to any treatment by booking a first visit.

mainEntity.name: Can I see Dr. Swati if I am not trying to conceive?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. EVE looks after PCOS, periods, endometriosis, fibroids, contraception, menopause and preventive care, as well as fertility. Many patients come for women's health concerns with no plan for pregnancy.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to bring my partner?

acceptedAnswer.text: For fertility problems, a first visit with both partners is the most useful, because the male partner's semen analysis is one of the first tests. For other concerns, you can come alone.

mainEntity.name: Are tests done on the same day?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many scans can be done at the visit. Blood tests and some procedures are planned for specific days of your cycle. Dr. Swati explains the timing so you do not make extra trips.

mainEntity.name: Do you offer treatment in a single visit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some concerns, such as a simple review or a scan, can be settled in one visit. Fertility care usually takes a few visits over one or two cycles, because tests and treatment are timed to your cycle.

mainEntity.name: At what age should a girl first see a gynaecologist?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no fixed age. A first reproductive health visit between 13 and 15 is suggested by some experts, and sooner if there are problems such as very painful periods, very heavy bleeding, or no periods by 15. Many girls need only a conversation.

mainEntity.name: Will my daughter need an internal examination?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rarely. Most teenage concerns are assessed by talking, a general check and, if needed, an abdominal ultrasound. An internal examination is done only when it is clearly necessary and with the young person's agreement. We explain first.

mainEntity.name: My daughter's periods are irregular. Is this normal?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is common for the first two years after periods begin. Cycles can range from about 21 to 45 days. See a doctor if periods are very heavy, come with severe pain, stop for 3 months, or have not begun by 15.

mainEntity.name: Can a teenager come alone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Patients under 18 attend with a parent or guardian, who gives consent. The teenager can also speak with the doctor alone for part of the visit. This helps young people ask honestly.

mainEntity.name: Is PCOS common in teenagers?

acceptedAnswer.text: PCOS can begin in the teen years, but diagnosis needs care, as irregular periods and acne can also be normal in early puberty. Dr. Swati uses age-appropriate criteria and avoids over-labelling. Lifestyle support helps either way.

mainEntity.name: Should my daughter get the HPV vaccine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it is best given early. India's national programme now offers a free single dose to 14-year-old girls, and private vaccination is available for other ages. Dr. Swati advises on the plan. See the HPV vaccination page.

@graph.name: Pap Smear and HPV Vaccine in Bangalore | EVE, Gunjur

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a Pap smear and an HPV test?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Pap smear looks at cervical cells under a microscope for abnormal changes. An HPV test looks for the virus that causes those changes. Many programmes use the HPV test first from age 30. Dr. Swati recommends the test, or both together, based on your age and history.

mainEntity.name: At what age should I start Pap smears?

acceptedAnswer.text: India's national programme targets women 30 to 65. Many gynaecologists start earlier based on risk. If you have been sexually active, or have a history of abnormal tests, a weak immune system or HIV, ask Dr. Swati when to begin.

mainEntity.name: How often should I be screened?

acceptedAnswer.text: If the results are normal, many guidelines advise repeating a Pap smear every 3 years, or an HPV test every 5 years. Your schedule may be different if you have had abnormal results. Dr. Swati sets your interval.

mainEntity.name: Does the HPV vaccine cause infertility?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. There is no evidence that the HPV vaccine affects fertility. It is non-live and has been used safely in many countries for years. It protects against infection linked to cervical cancer.

mainEntity.name: I am already married or older. Is the vaccine still useful?

acceptedAnswer.text: It may be, though benefit is greatest before exposure. Women up to 26, and in some cases older, can be vaccinated. Screening remains important. Dr. Swati can advise based on your age and history.

mainEntity.name: What does an abnormal Pap smear mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: An abnormal result usually means cell changes, not cancer. Most are caused by HPV and are mild. You may need an HPV test, a colposcopy and sometimes a biopsy. Early changes are treatable, and this is exactly what screening aims to find.

mainEntity.name: Which contraceptive method should I choose?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single right method for everyone. The right one depends on your health, your periods, whether you want to conceive soon, how often you can remember a pill, and your comfort. Dr. Swati reviews your history and explains the options so you can choose.

mainEntity.name: Does contraception affect fertility later?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Pills, IUDs and implants are reversible, and ovulation usually returns within a few months of stopping. The injection can delay return to regular cycles for several months. Age and other health factors matter more for fertility than past contraception.

mainEntity.name: Is emergency contraception safe, and when should I take it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Emergency contraception pills are safe and work best the sooner they are taken after unprotected sex, within 72 to 120 hours depending on the type. A copper IUD placed within 5 days is the most effective form. They do not end an existing pregnancy.

mainEntity.name: Can I use contraception while breastfeeding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The progestin-only pill, IUDs, implants and condoms are suitable. Estrogen-containing methods are usually delayed for several weeks after delivery. Dr. Swati chooses with you based on how recently you gave birth.

mainEntity.name: Can contraception help with PCOS or heavy periods?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some can. Combined pills and hormonal IUDs reduce heavy bleeding and can regulate cycles in PCOS, and some reduce acne. They do not cure PCOS, and stopping may bring symptoms back. See the PCOS and Menstrual disorders pages.

mainEntity.name: Can a young or unmarried woman get advice here?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Contraceptive counselling is private and given without judgment to any adult. Teenagers are welcome with a parent or guardian, and may also speak to the doctor alone for part of the visit. See Adolescent gynaecology.

@graph.name: Early Pregnancy Scan in Bangalore | EVE, Gunjur

mainEntity.name: When should I have my first pregnancy scan?

acceptedAnswer.text: About 6 weeks after the first day of your last period, which is roughly 2 weeks after a missed period. A heartbeat is usually visible by then. If you have pain, bleeding, a past ectopic pregnancy or fertility treatment, Dr. Swati may scan earlier.

mainEntity.name: Can an early scan miss a pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: A very early scan can show nothing even when you are pregnant, because the structures are tiny. If the scan is inconclusive, a repeat scan in about a week, and sometimes a blood hCG test, answers the question.

mainEntity.name: Is a transvaginal scan safe in early pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. It uses sound waves, not radiation, and does not harm the pregnancy. The probe is covered, cleaned between patients, and placed gently. You can ask for the scan to stop at any time.

mainEntity.name: When can a heartbeat be seen?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually at about 6 weeks, sometimes at 5.5 to 7 weeks, depending on your dates. If the scan is too early, no heartbeat does not mean a problem. A repeat scan about a week later is usual.

mainEntity.name: Do you tell the baby's sex?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Telling the sex of the baby is prohibited under the PCPNDT Act, and EVE never does it. Scans at the clinic are for location, growth, number and heartbeat.

mainEntity.name: I had a miscarriage before. Can I come for an early scan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. An early scan can reassure you, and Dr. Swati can plan extra care. If you have had two or more losses, see Recurrent pregnancy loss for evaluation, ideally before the next pregnancy.
